To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

children with higher fat mass have a higher retinal venular caliber and lower arteriolar to venular ratio, especially in boys, and that changes in fat mass are positively related to the retinal venular diameter over time.
children with high fat mass have an altered retinal microvascualture, especially in boys.
changes in body composition over a 7 year period are associated with the CRV in children, especially in boys.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the retinal microvascular structure and body fat in children.
the early detection of cardiovascular disease in childhood.
the relationship between the retinal microcirculation and body fat in childhood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
body fat is associated with retinal microvascular changes in children, especially in boys, and that these changes are more pronounced in those who gain fat mass during childhood.
body fat evolution during childhood may be associated with retinal microvascualture in boys.
the retinal microvascular changes may represent underlying mechanisms through which changes in body fat over time contributes to cardiovascular disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the retinal microvascular changes in children with higher body fat are already present and are more pronounced in boys.
changes in fat mass are associated with changes in the retinal venular diameter, but not in the retinal arteriular diameter.
children with high fat mass have a more developed retinal microvascular network (CRVE) and a less developed retinal microvascular network (CRAE).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the microvasculature may be an important mechanism through which childhood obesity may affect cardiovascular disease later in life.
changes in body composition during childhood may have an important impact on the cardiovascular health of the next generation.
body fat is a more accurate predictor of retinal vascular changes than BMI.
